en: The Sixth: Contemplating the Realm of Dhyāna-Samādhi, as spoken by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai during the Sui Dynasty and recorded by his disciple Guanding.
Now, chronic illness and long-distance travel are obstacles to dhyāna-samādhi. [They] are established...
The *Lokaprajñapti-abhidharma* states:
"Frequent quarreling and frequent involvement in worldly affairs are also obstacles to meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*).
Furthermore, excessive recitation and study are also obstacles to meditative concentration."
The *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-bodhicitta-sūtra* states:
"There are thirty-six defilements of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
These defilements are themselves hindrances."
When one has entered the aforementioned stages and reached the Cool Lake,
once the entry into the stream is complete, there is no further need to contemplate the meditative objects.
However, even if demonic obstacles have been transcended, true illumination may not yet have arisen.
Although there is no separate cultivation because it is cultivated through general practice,
past habitual tendencies toward the various dhyānas arise and manifest profusely;
one should regard these as the deeds of Māra and remain observant regarding the various dhyānas.
Why is this? Because the exquisite and subtle bliss of dhyāna gives rise to attachment and relish, causing defilement to increase day by day;
to claim that this is the Path is to fall into overweening pride (adhimāna).
If one scorns and abandons it, one completely loses the skillful means.
Such faults as these cannot be fully recorded.
Although one may escape the harm of Māra, one becomes further bound by meditative concentration.
Just as it is of no benefit to fall into water while avoiding fire,
one must contemplate the meditative objects for this reason;
however, the various dhyāna factors and concentrations that aid the path possess great power.
Both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras alike praise them.
The four dhyānas and eight samādhis are explained in detail in the Abhidharma and the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*.
The nine dhyānas of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) are clarified in the *Bhūmisaṃgraha*, and the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are most clearly elucidated in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.
Now, I shall briefly indicate the characteristics of its manifestation,
roughly categorized into four points.
The first clarifies the opening and closing [of the gates].
Second, the causes and conditions for its arousal;
third, the characteristics of its arousal;
fourth, the cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
First, to clarify the opening and closing [of the gates]:
although the methods of the Chan gate are immeasurable, they are provisionally categorized into ten gates.
The first is the four fundamental dhyānas.
Twenty-six: the special victories; twenty-seven:
the three clear knowledges;
twenty-eight: the nine perceptions.
5. The eight liberations (aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ).
6. The six impurities of the great elements (ṣaḍ mahābhūta-aśubhāḥ).
7. The mind of loving-kindness (maitrīcitta).
Eight causes and conditions;
nine, mindfulness of the Buddha;
ten, supernormal powers.
How do these ten gates compare with the five gates and the fifteen gates?
They differ only in terms of expansion and contraction.
To expand the five into ten is as follows:
By opening up *ānāpāna-smṛti*, one produces the *viśeṣa-uttara* and *abhibhvāyatana*.
By opening up *aśubha-bhāvanā*, one produces the *vimokṣas* and *mahā-aśubha*.
Through the causal conditions of *maitrī-citta*, one maintains the fundamental basis.
In the Abhidharma, the gate of mindfulness of the Buddha is called the "expedient means of the elements" (*dhātu-upāya*); in the *Dhyāna-sūtra*, it is termed "mindfulness of the Buddha.
Both of these likewise maintain the fundamental principle.
The supernormal powers (abhijñā) arise based on the nine dhyānas and do not depend exclusively on a single method.
As for the consolidation of fifteen gates into ten,
the three rules for each of breath-counting (ānāpāna-smṛti) and impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā) would not be consistent [if they were not so merged].
The three types of loving-kindness are combined into one,
which is the loving-kindness toward sentient beings (*sattva-maitrī*).
This is because two names have been subsumed.
Dhyāna is the gateway for the sequential investigation of phenomena.
Contemplation with conditions is the entry into the realization of principle for the two vehicles;
contemplation without conditions is the entry into the realization of principle for the Mahāyāna.
There is no principle for discarding two while retaining one.
If they were to be opened up,
they would be subsumed within the two objects of the Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas.
The conditions (pratyaya) also consist of three gates:
the revolving of the three periods of time is coarse;
the meaning of the maturation of fruit (vipāka-phala) being manifest in a single thought-moment is subtle.
Because they are subtle, they are attached to principle; because they are coarse, they belong to phenomena.
Now, omitting the subtle and retaining only the coarse, we simply refer to them as the "gates of the three periods.
Although mindfulness of the Buddha is also threefold, we take only the mindfulness of the Responsive Buddha (saṃbuddha).
Regarding "supernormal powers" (abhijñā), one should take only the five supernormal powers.
If one takes only the five gates, there will be things not included;
if one takes the fifteen meanings, they will be confused with the underlying principle (tattva).
Therefore, while the principles are simplified and the phenomena are expanded—
such that although the methods of opening and closing differ, each possesses its own intended meaning—
the next section clarifies the outflowing (*āsrava*) and the non-outflowing (*anāsrava*).
If one follows the Abhidharma, these ten dhyānas are all classified as contaminated (sāsrava).
Only that which is cultivated through the wisdom that takes the Truths as its object is called uncontaminated (anāsrava) dhyāna;
it is not otherwise.
However, when cultivation is based solely on conditioned phenomena (*vastu*), it is called "tainted dhyāna" (*sāsrava-dhyāna*).
The *Abhidharmakośa* (Treatise on the Treasury) is likewise:
the fundamental [dhyānas] and so forth are tainted.
Cultivating the mind of emptiness and signlessness is called "outflow-free" (anāsrava).
Now, this differs slightly from that:
the essential nature of the ten dhyānas is here considered to be "with outflows" (sāsrava).
This is the meditation on such matters.
If a melon could serve as a causal condition for a feverish illness,
it should be analyzed in detail.
The four dhyānas have existed in the world from the beginning and are shared by ordinary people and non-Buddhists;
those who practice them exclusively only generate out-flowing (sāsrava) states.
As for practicing the twelve gates oneself and transforming others through praise of the Dharma—this is what is meant by "praising."
The Great Sūtra states:
"That which is called forty-eight years" refers precisely to this meaning.
The Sixteen Superiorities and the Universal Clarity:
even ordinary persons of sharp faculties cultivate this dhyāna when a Buddha has not appeared in the world,
yet they do not give rise to the outflow-free (anāsrava) state.
If the Tathāgata speaks, it also gives rise to the outflow-free (anāsrava).
Compared to other dhyānas, although its power is weak, it nonetheless surpasses the fundamental [dhyāna].
For this reason, it is said to be both with-outflows (sāsrava) and without-outflows (anāsrava).
The nine notions (*navasaṃjñā*) and so forth are supramundane adventitious dharmas;
although they are mundane phenomena, they are capable of preventing the faults of desire and do not depend on the wisdom of the [Four] Truths to give rise to the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state.
For example, when the five hundred arhats of Kāṭhina each preached the Four Noble Truths seven times to every person,
they were still unable to realize the Way.
The Buddha taught that the contemplation of impurity immediately gives rise to the untainted (anāsrava).
Because the power of revulsion is so strong, it is classified as belonging to the untainted.
If one were to say it is not untainted, [it would contradict this].
One should not refer to them as "noble" (ārya) precepts, concentration, and wisdom.
As for the term "noble," it signifies "correct" (samyak); how could "correct" exceed the untainted (anāsrava)?
As a Great Sūtra says:
The noble practice is the realm of all Buddhas;
it is not something known by the followers of the two vehicles.
Because the Buddha taught this Dharma and the followers of the two vehicles practice it accordingly, it is called the "noble practice."
Now, the Buddha has taught that the Noble Dharma is practiced by those of the Two Vehicles;
how could it not be untainted (*anāsrava*)?
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
The fundamental is the gift of worldly dharmas;
impurity and so forth are the gift of supramundane dharmas.
Since it is said to be supramundane, how could it not be untainted (*anāsrava*)?
It is further said:
"The nine perceptions open the way to impurity;
impurity opens the way to the foundation of mindfulness of the body."
The foundation of mindfulness of the body opens up the [other] three foundations of mindfulness;
the three foundations of mindfulness open up the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;
and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment open up nirvana.
Is it not the case that the primary condition for nirvana is untainted (anāsrava)?
If you say that "substantial dhyāna" (vastu-dhyāna) must be tainted (sāsrava),
it is like taking two medicinal stones, one hot and one cold.
Although they share the same object of meditation, there is a distinction between those with outflows (*sāsrava*) and those without outflows (*anāsrava*).

If that which takes an outflow-free object is called "outflow-free," then the six stages eliminate the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-heya*), while the seven stages eliminate the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
This is also a conditioned object and should likewise be untainted (*anāsrava*).

For those who sever the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*) in the sixth and seventh stages, they never employ the fundamental [concentrations] alone; rather, they must necessarily rely on the knowledge of the truths (*satya-jñāna*) to manifest within these states.
The fundamental [meditations] used alone do not have the uncontaminated as their object;
this is not the case for the [contemplations on] impurity and so forth,
which can directly serve as conditions through impurity itself, and so on.
The reason why the ten perceptions are not included is that the first three pertain to the vision of the truths,
while the middle four pertain to contemplation.
The final three [categories] belong to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); because they are all subsumed under the category of ultimate reality (*tattva*), they are not included.
As for the non-inclusion of the eight recollections (*aṣṭānusmṛti*):
There are those who cultivate the nine perceptions without fear;
furthermore, because they have already been subsumed within the mindfulness of the Buddha, they are not taken up [separately].
The contemplation of loving-kindness belongs to both categories.
If loving-kindness arises based on the fundamental [dhyānas], it belongs to the out-flowing (sāsrava) category;
if it arises based on [meditations such as] the foul (aśubha), it belongs to the non-out-flowing (anāsrava) category.
Regarding the stages of loving-kindness, there are distinctions according to the levels of the meditative grounds.
Based on the fundamental [meditations], one achieves the object-condition of sentient beings;
based on the liberations (vimokṣa), one achieves the object-condition of dharmas.
There is no other stage for the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya).
The five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) associated with the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*) are all categorized according to other stages;
for example, it is said that the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrīcitta*) belongs to two [categories], and so forth.
Next, the underlying intentions (*āśaya*) differ.
Question:
Regarding these ten gates, how do they compare in terms of similarities and differences with the sequential meditation gate (*anupūrva-dhyāna-mukha*) and the counteractive methods (*pratipakṣa*)?
Answer: The sequential gates of dhyāna are for the sake of accomplishing the dhyāna-pāramitā,
because the roots of goodness of dhyāna are sharp.
In the Chan school, one first gives rise to [the mind] and later verifies its good or evil;
herein, for the sake of accomplishing prajñā,
the roots of goodness in Chan are dull.
First, one is obstructed by afflictions, encounters karma, and meets with Māra;
only later does one initiate dhyāna.
During the process of antidotes, one cultivates the factors conducive to awakening (bodhipākṣika-dharma) in order to destroy these hindrances.
Now, this [state] arises spontaneously of itself;
nevertheless, it remains an object of contemplation.
Although the Chan gate is the same, each possesses its own specific intent, and so forth.
Next, to clarify the differences in depth and shallowness:
the four dhyānas are fundamental, darkly realized, and savoring meditations (āsvādanasamāpatti).
They are accessible to both ordinary persons and noble ones alike, being attained through even slight cultivation.
It is particularly superior.
It possesses a rare wisdom of contemplation that is neither savoring nor obscured,
and it corresponds horizontally to the foundations of mindfulness while corresponding vertically to the fundamental [dhyānas].
Therefore, flavor comes first and purity follows.
This collectively clarifies that the characteristics of realization through contemplative wisdom are profound and subtle;
subsequently, it refers to the totality. These three are identical as the fundamental, actual contemplation.
The power to subdue delusions is weak.
The nine perceptions (navasaṃjñā) are precisely the initial gateway of conceptual visualization;
because they serve as the vanguard that suppresses desire, they are listed next.
The nine perceptions merely engender revulsion toward external objects but have not yet disciplined the mind;
therefore, they are followed by the eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*).
Although these liberations destroy both internal and external desire, they do so in a general manner rather than in detail.
Because one cannot attain mastery over conditions,
the next section clarifies the "Great Impurity" (mahā-aśubha) to destroy craving for both the physical body and its environment.
Although this generally and specifically treats greed, one has not yet cultivated great merit.
Therefore, it is followed by the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Although one may internally subdue heavy greed and externally cultivate merit,
if one does not enter into dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), it is not the right view of the world.
Therefore, next is dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

The wheeling through the three periods of time, being without a master and without a self, constitutes right view of the world. Although it is right view of the world, [it is not yet the ultimate truth].
This is because the power of merit from the lower causes is weak,
whereas the power of merit from the higher fruits is vast; thus,
although the various meditative concentrations mentioned previously [are attained],...
Because they do not yet possess the power of mastery over transformation,
it is followed by the supernormal powers (abhijñā), and so forth.
Next, there are differences in their mutual arousal.
Their sequential mutual arising consists of eight types in total; this may be understood by analogy with the aggregates (*skandha*),
elements (*dhātu*), and sense objects (*viṣaya*), and so forth.
Second, regarding the clarification of the causes and conditions for the arousal of dhyāna:
The Mahāyāna Sūtra states,
"All sentient beings possess the 'taste of the first stage' dhyāna."
Whether one cultivates them or not, they will certainly be attained.
Judging from immediate circumstances, one may not cultivate them until the end of the kalpa;
yet, when traced back over vast eons, it has been seen that one has already been free from the hindrances.
It is like reciting the scriptures:
if one neglects them for a short time, they are easy to resume;
if one neglects them for a long time, they are difficult to resume.
One should know that there was sequential training in the past;
thus, they arise sequentially, and so forth,
up to the cultivation of the matter and the arising of the matter, and so on.
Just as when the great earth is fully endowed with its various types and receives the moistening vapor of rain, each thing sprouts and grows;
yet their growth and the ripening of their fruits do not occur simultaneously, but rather in succession.
The plum ripens in the fourth month, the peach in the seventh, the pear in the ninth, and the persimmon in the tenth.
Although the conditions for their growth through rain are the same, there are differences in how they form their fruit.
Past habituation is like a seed.
Calm abiding and insight are like rain;
the arising of meditative concentration is like the ripening of fruit at varying stages.
Generally speaking, there are eight types.
This is called the arising of internal conditions.
Furthermore, although there may be wholesome states ready to arise,
they must depend upon majestic spiritual power to be brought forth.
Although the earth possesses the seed, it will not sprout without the sun.
The Buddha is free from hatred and attachment; he benefits all universally according to conditions.
If there is a sequential condition, he bestows grace accordingly.
Even down to the practice of taking phenomena as conditions, one simply adds cultivation to the phenomena themselves.
It is like a great bell that awaits being struck; whether the sound is great or small depends on the mallet.
This added cultivation is always equal, regardless of whether the depth or shallowness of the practice is heard or cultivated.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"A lotus in a pond cannot endure being shaded from the sun; it will undoubtedly wither and die.
Likewise, if goodness is not augmented, one will remain submerged and fail to manifest."
The Jingdu jing (Sutra on Pure Deliverance) states:
"Sentient beings deliver themselves;
the Buddha is of no benefit to them."
The Bodhisattva Pure Deliverance said,
"If sentient beings do not hear the twelve divisions of the Buddha's sutras,
how can they attain deliverance?"
The two statements, though seemingly contradictory, together form a single meaning;
this is called "arising through external conditions.
Third, the characteristics of the arising of the various dhyānas are as follows:
If one considers the *pratyutpanna-samādhi*, the arousal of the root [of practice] is slight;
for those who practice constant sitting (*nitya-prahāṇika*) and so forth, it is abundant.
For now, let us discuss this in terms of sitting.
If the body is upright, the mind collected, and the breath harmonized,
one perceives that the path of this mind becomes submerged in profound stillness;
it settles into a state of tranquil security, entering step by step.
When the mind dwells upon its object without wandering or scattering,
this is called "coarse abiding" (audārikasthiti).
Following this state of mind, it becomes increasingly tranquil and superior to what preceded it.
This is called "subtle abiding.
Between the preceding and succeeding moments of the two minds, there must necessarily be a dharma that sustains the body.
When this dharma arises, the body naturally becomes upright.
It is neither fatiguing nor painful;
it is as if some object were supporting one's physical strength.
However, if it is held improperly, when it is brought [into position], it is urgent and intensely painful.
To be lax and weary when departing is a coarse and inferior way of maintaining the Dharma.
One who maintains the Dharma well maintains both the coarse and the subtle abidings without the fault of being either too relaxed or too hurried.
Or for one or two moments,
or for one or two days,
or for one or two months.
One gradually perceives a deeper subtlety;
suddenly, the ground of the mind becomes partially opened and clarified.
The body is like a cloud or a shadow, radiantly bright and pure.
In conjunction with the factors conducive to meditative concentration, one maintains the mind without wavering;
harboring a state of pure elimination that is refreshing and cool,
and though following along with emptiness and purity, one still perceives the signs of body and mind.
When the qualities of the constituent factors have not yet arisen,
this is called the concentration of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*).
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* refers to this as the mind associated with the ten wholesome courses of action.
That which flickers and glitters should not endure for long.
Now it is said:
when one’s resolve is weak and unstable, like unbaked clay, it is called "flickering."
It is not necessarily like a lamp flame.
Furthermore, regarding its being called "a flash of lightning," that treatise states:
Question: Beyond the seven [dhyānas], are there further concentrations that can give rise to the outflow-free (anāsrava)? Answer: Yes;
the desire-realm concentration (kāmadhātu-samādhi) can give rise to the outflow-free.
The outflow-free [wisdom] arises swiftly, like a flash of lightning.
If one does not give rise to the outflow-free state while remaining [in the meditative state], the duration will be long; as the *Śāsana-avaśeṣa* states:
"If one sees the flash of lightning, one may momentarily attain the Path of Vision."
For example, when Ānanda was unable to arouse his mind through exertion,
he relaxed his mind and took up his pillow, whereupon he immediately entered the "lightning-flash" (*vidyut-prabhā*) samādhi; this lightning-flash is also the Vajra.
The Vajra is not solitary because it enters the outflow-free state from the desire realm.
Its rapid manifestation is likened to a flash of lightning;
it is not that this name is obtained solely through the meditative concentration of the desire realm.
Abiding in the concentration of the desire realm for months or years,
one maintains the mind through the power of meditative absorption without laxity or pain;
it is even possible to remain thus for days on end without emerging.
Following this state of mind, there occurs a sudden, total transformation.
One becomes vast and empty, no longer perceiving the body, head, clothing, or bedding within the dhyāna-concentration of desire;
it is like the open expanse of space, brilliantly clear and profoundly peaceful.
The body is an obstacle to the matter; this obstacle obstructs the future.
Once the obstacle has departed and the body is empty, the future [realization] can arise.
This is called the sign of the stage of "not yet reached" (anāgamya-bhūmi).
Those who lack true understanding may attain this concentration and claim it is the "patience regarding non-arising" (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti).
Yet, since their innate obstructions remain and they have not yet entered the first dhyāna,
how could they erroneously call it the "concentration of non-arising"?
Just as a fool might lightly step upon fire covered by ashes, so it is with those who rely on the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, which holds that there is no future dhyāna;
therefore, it says:
"You claim there is a future dhyāna."
This is likely not what I intended by the "dhyāna of desire.
However, according to the Abhidharma, the Venerable Ghoṣaka maintains that it exists.
The *Śāstra* (the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*) sets them forth in full detail;
while the Buddha provided both explanations, the Master [Asaṅga] has here specifically expounded one.
Now, I shall judge each case according to the individual.
Having personally attained the concentration of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*) and remained therein for many months without yet reaching the "not-yet-arrived" stage (*anāgamya*),
he soon entered the first dhyāna.
This is merely referred to as the "desire realm" and not specifically as the "not-yet-arrived" stage.
There are those who dwell in the desire realm for no long time;
because they have not yet completed ten days [there],
it is said they have "not yet arrived" rather than being described as being in the "desire realm."
There are those who possess both dharmas for a long duration;
therefore, it is said that the two determinations cannot be judged one-sidedly.
Now, I shall set them forth in full according to the *Mahā-śāstra*.
The characteristics of the correct and the deviant at each stage are explained in detail within the section on cultivation and realization;
however, since the first dhyāna is proximate to the desire realm,
one must have a general understanding of its many difficulties, much like a border region with many hardships.
From the initial stage of coarse abiding up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there are generally four divisions:
falling back, guarding, abiding, and advancing.
Furthermore, the division of falling back is twofold.
First, spontaneous regression;
second, regression due to conditions and contact.
Conditions are of two kinds: internal and external.
The twenty-five types of errors in exhalation and inhalation regarding external skillful means constitute "retrogression through contact with external conditions.
Within the state of meditative stillness, there are the three obstacles and the four māras.
From this, sorrow and craving arise;
this is called the internal condition for the decline of contact.
Later, one may again cultivate and attain it.
Or, even when practicing, many people fail to attain it.
As for the factor of protection,
one skillfully employs both internal and external expedient means.
One protects and sustains the concentrated mind so as not to let it be lost.
Regarding the factor of stability (*sthiti-bhāga*): it may arise from guarding [the mind] so that it remains secure and is not lost.
Alternatively, abiding spontaneously of itself is the "abiding portion.
As for the "progressing portion":
Whether it be spontaneous progress or diligent exertion,
each has its own horizontal and vertical dimensions.
Both the horizontal and vertical [approaches] each have gradual and sudden modes.
If one progresses through each of the twelve gates one by one, this is called gradual progress.
If one is complete all at once, this is called sudden progress.
When the *viśeṣa* (special) and *abhijñā-pratibhāna* (super-knowledge and eloquence) arise chapter by chapter, this is called horizontal gradualism (*tiryak-śanaiḥ*).
When they arise all at once, this is called horizontal suddenness (*tiryak-sadyas*).
Furthermore, within each of the four divisions, there are likewise four divisions.
This is as explained in detail in the section on cultivation and realization, and so forth.
Now, to discuss the progressive stages according to the vertical perspective:
from the *anāgamya-samādhi* (the preparatory stage of the first dhyāna), one gradually perceives the body and mind as empty and quiescent.
Internally one does not see the body, and externally one does not see objects;
for a day, or even for months and years, the concentrated mind remains unbroken.
Within this meditative absorption, one perceives that the body and mind are subtly vibrating.
It moves continuously from moment to moment;
it may manifest as movement, itching, heaviness, lightness, cold, warmth, roughness, or smoothness.
Some people say:
The subtle matter of the mind-sphere contacts the pure matter of the form realm within the body of the desire realm;
for example, just as the pure matter of the desire realm exists above the sense organs and possesses the functions of seeing and hearing.
If, according to this meaning, contact comes from the outside,
it would imply that all sentient beings possess the dhyāna of the "taste of the first stage" (āsvādana-dhyāna),
just as a wealthy man has a blind son or as there is fire within bamboo.
The afflictions within the mind do not arise simultaneously;
meditation is likewise.
When coarse obstructions of phenomena exist, one cannot give rise to it.
Now, as one cultivates the mind, it gradually becomes sharp;
though the obstacles of one's nature have been removed, subtle phenomena still arise.
Why must these necessarily come from without?
Why is this? Counting the breaths can transform the mind; when the mind is transformed, the fire is transformed.
Fire transforms into wind;
wind transforms into water; water transforms into earth.
Because the four great elements transform into subtle states, there are eight tactile sensations.
It is like barley transforming into malt,
the malt transforming into dregs,
and the dregs transforming into wine.
Dregs are a metaphor for the concentration of desire;
wine is a metaphor for the first dhyāna.
Since the grain is the basis, it does not come from without.
If one were to dogmatically insist that [the argument] comes from outside oneself, one would fall into the error of attributing it to both self and other natures.
Now, having completed the refutation of the four natures according to the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*,
this [argument] merely emerges from within the treatise itself.
Furthermore, among the eight types of tangibles, these are the four great elements:
motion and lightness are wind;
itching and warmth are fire.
Coldness and smoothness are the water element;
heaviness and roughness are the earth element.
When their essential natures and functions are combined, there are thus eight tangibles.
When a tactile sensation arises through movement,
it may begin from the head, back, waist, ribs, feet, or other parts,
gradually spreading throughout the entire body.
Within the body one perceives movement, yet externally there is no sign of motion;
it is as if a wind has arisen, moving subtly and continuously from head to foot,
for the most part resulting in a state of decline.
The waist gives rise to the factors of abiding and maintenance;
the feet give rise mostly to the factor of progress;
and movement brings about the merit of the forest of branches of contact.
The merits are briefly stated as tenfold:
emptiness, clarity, meditative concentration, wisdom, and a virtuous mind;
together with flexibility, joy, bliss, and liberation, they correspond to the sphere of the objective realm.
Regarding "emptiness":
when movement and contact are triggered, the empty mind becomes vast and open,
no longer the same as it was previously when its inherent obstructions had not been removed.
"Clarity" means it is brilliant,
pure, exquisite, and resplendent beyond compare.
"Concentration" means...
With a single-minded tranquility and without any distraction or agitation,
the wise one—
No longer deluded or obscured by the net of doubt, the mind attains tranquility and benefit.
One with a virtuous mind feels shame, remorse, faith, and reverence, thinking: "I have never before attained this Dharma."

Therefore, it is called "reversal" (*prātikūlya*).
This also concerns the general and specific characteristics, and so forth.
If this is the great contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), why would the impurities flow only from the primary retribution (*vipāka*)?
The conditioned environment— dwellings, houses, money, wealth, grain, clothing, food, drink, mountains,
rivers, gardens, groves, the Yangtze and Huai rivers, ponds, and marshes—
all material phenomena whatsoever are entirely impure.
Worms and pus flow out, the place reeks with a rank and putrid odor;
the house is like a burial mound, the coins are like dead snakes;
the soup is like excrement broth, and the rice is like white worms.
Their robes are like stinking hides; their mountains are like heaps of flesh;
their ponds are like rivers of pus; their groves and forests are like withered bones;
and their rivers and seas are like pools of filth.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra says:
"To regard delicious soup as foul-smelling liquid is precisely this contemplation.
During seated meditation, one may suddenly perceive it in this manner.
Seeing that this great earth has not a single excellent spot,
and that neither the physical body nor its environment can be craved again—
this is called the arising of the "Great Impurity," like a fire first breaking out.
When effort is applied, the smoke and flames intensify until they obscure all minute details.
Once the fire has gained momentum, it no longer requires specific fuel;
it can even dry up rivers and streams.
At first, one contemplates impurity by focusing on a single corpse within a single country;
thus, the lustful mind alternately arises and subsides.
Now that the power of meditative concentration has been established and the sense of revulsion has also intensified,
all things— both the environment and its inhabitants— are nothing but impure;
thus, the desire-mind is forever stilled.
Furthermore, what fixed characteristic do all things possess?
They are perceived differently according to the karmic retribution of individuals:
pure forms are perceived through the maturation of wholesome karma, while impure forms are perceived through the maturation of unwholesome karma.
Just as the various celestial jewels, jeweled palaces, and human wealth and pleasures exist,
one who grasps tiles and stones transforms them into gold and silver;
through the power of virtue, both the environment and its inhabitants are rendered pure.
As described in the *Saṃgharakṣita-sūtra*,
the characteristics of the hells vary; in some,
one sees one's own flesh being turned into earth and plowed by others.
Alternatively, one may see the body as a forest broken and crushed by many;
or the body as a mountain, a house, or a garment—
altogether one hundred and twenty such forms.
All these are impure forms summoned by the retribution of evil karma;
if one clings to these pure forms with firm attachment and love,
one must use the power of great contemplation to shatter this great attachment.
This overturns great perversity and establishes the contemplation of great impurity. Why is this?
For the nature of illusory arts is largely that of deception.
One who attains mastery over the principles of the supernormal powers (abhijñā-dharma) can transform all things.
It is like ghee, wax, gold, or iron, which undergo transformation when they encounter heat.
Just as water encounters cold and becomes earth,
this attainment of insight conforms to the way of transformation;
such is the power of meditative concentration.
If the fundamental [attainments] merely eliminate attachment to lower stages but cannot eliminate that of their own stage,
then the small and great liberations (vimokṣa) are not yet untainted (anāsrava).
However, one merely eliminates the attachments of the lower stages and of one's own stage.
If the object is untainted (*anāsrava*), then through universal application, one eliminates attachment from both the lower and the upper stages.
If a person generates great impurity (*aśubha*) and enters into the liberations (*vimokṣa*), that too is "great."
It is subsumed under the first dhyāna.
If one internally visualizes the skeleton and externally contemplates the eight colors, as well as both the primary and secondary retributions,
it is because the objects of focus are vast.
This is called the second great liberation (*mahā-vimokṣa*).
It is subsumed under the second dhyāna.
If one enters the pure liberation from the great impurity, that too is "great."
This applies up to the liberation through cessation as well.
As for the great bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*),
they further ripen the liberations.
This enables mastery over the transformation of conditions,
as clarified in the *Mahā-śāstra*. It explains that even a person of dull faculties, having completed the cultivation of the eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*), [attains this].
One then cultivates the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
Having completed the cultivation of the three liberations (*vimokṣa*),
one cultivates the spheres of mastery and so forth within the four dhyānas.
Those of superior faculties cultivate only the first liberation (prathama-vimokṣa), which is itself the cultivation of all dharmas.

Again, this is based on the distinction between the primary and secondary [bodies]:
one corpse constitutes "few," while two corpses constitute "many.
This successive transmission may be understood in this manner.
A single robe, a single meal, or a single mountain and river are considered few;
immeasurable robes, meals, mountains, and rivers are considered many.
When first beginning practice, one proceeds from the few toward the many.
Now, the arising [of the body] should also be understood in this way.
Regarding whether it is beautiful or ugly:
virtuous karma resulting in physical symmetry is "beautiful."
Evil karma is base and ugly;
these two are both considered beautiful by me where they are good,
and ugly where they are evil.
In both of these cases, possessing wisdom is good,
while possessing folly is ugly.
In both of these cases, wealth and status are good.
Poverty and low status are considered ugly.
Thus, both beauty and ugliness are impure;
so too are mountains, rivers, nations, food, clothing, and dwellings.
Whether beautiful or ugly, both are impure.
Furthermore, both the primary body and its secondary parts are ugly;
yet the eight-colored rays emitted by the skeleton person are considered beautiful.
Furthermore, the eight forms that are ugly are refined into beauty;
yet both the beautiful and the ugly are impure.
These two spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) are subsumed within the first dhyāna.
If one is internally without the perception of form,
one perceives external forms, whether many or few, beautiful or ugly,
with superior knowledge and superior vision.
Within the skeleton that has been extinguished internally, there are eight external colors.
Furthermore, there are variations in the number and quality of the primary and secondary elements (the person and their environment),
as previously explained in detail.
